title: Min–max principles for singular values
subtitle: G2 lecture 052000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: The eigenvalue min–max theorem answers a question about a self-adjoint operator: if we are allowed to choose a subspace, how large or small can its quadratic form be on unit vectors in that subspace?
body: We now ask a related question for any linear map. It need not be square. It need not be self-adjoint. We might map three-dimensional vectors into a space of five dimensions, or the other way around. There may be no eigenvalues that describe the map at all. But one measurement always makes sense. Give the map a unit input, and measure the length of its output. Which input directions produce large outputs?

slides.title: Recover the geometry from the singular-value decomposition
slides.lead: Let A be a linear map from a finite-dimensional inner-product space E into another such space F.
body: Let the dimension of E be n. The singular-value decomposition gives an orthonormal basis of E consisting of right singular vectors. Order their singular values from largest to smallest, including zeros if necessary. Call these singular values sigma one through sigma n. For a right singular vector v sub j, the length of A applied to that vector is sigma j. Images of right singular vectors associated to positive singular values point along mutually perpendicular left singular vectors. A right singular vector with zero singular value lies in the kernel. Take an arbitrary input x.

slides.title: Remove the strongest directions
slides.lead: Choose an integer j between one and n.
body: Imagine that an adversary is allowed to discard a subspace of dimension j minus one. We are then allowed to choose any remaining unit direction orthogonal to that discarded subspace. We choose the one on which A has the largest output length. The adversary wants to make that largest remaining length as small as possible. The minimum possible answer is sigma j. First prove that the adversary can achieve no more than sigma j. Discard the span of the first j minus one right singular vectors. Every unit vector in its orthogonal complement is a combination of right singular directions j through n. None has an output longer than sigma j.

slides.title: Keep a subspace instead
body: We are now allowed to choose a subspace of dimension j, and an adversary chooses the unit vector in that subspace on which A has the smallest output. We want that worst-case output length to be as large as possible. Again the answer is sigma j. For the lower bound, select the span of the first j right singular vectors. Every unit vector there has output length at least sigma j, so our best possible value is at least sigma j. For the upper bound, consider any j-dimensional subspace the chooser proposes. Look at the span of the right singular vectors numbered j through n. Its dimension is n minus j plus one. Those dimensions add up to n plus one.

slides.title: A rectangular example
slides.lead: Let A take a pair of real numbers, x and y, to the three-dimensional vector whose coordinates are five x, two y, and zero.
body: The source has dimension two. The right singular vectors are the ordinary horizontal and vertical unit vectors. Their singular values are five and two. The unused third output coordinate does not create a third right singular direction. For the first singular value, no directions are discarded. The largest output of a unit input has length five. For the second, discard one input direction. If we discard the horizontal direction, the surviving vertical unit vector has output length two.

slides.title: Connection to the modulus
slides.lead: Recall that the modulus of A is the positive square root of A adjoint composed with A.
body: It acts on the source space, and it has exactly the singular values of A as its eigenvalues. More importantly, the length of A x equals the length of the modulus applied to x. Consequently the variational games we just played are literally the Courant–Fischer games for this positive operator, expressed through lengths instead of Rayleigh quotients. For a unit vector, the square of the output length is the quadratic form of A adjoint A. We could first apply Courant–Fischer to the squared singular values, then take nonnegative square roots. That gives another proof of both formulas.

slides.title: A first approximation consequence
slides.lead: Suppose someone offers a map B whose rank is at most j minus one, claiming that B approximates A very well.
body: Because B has rank at most j minus one, its kernel has codimension at most j minus one. Our dimension argument shows that the kernel of B meets the span of the first j right singular vectors in a nonzero direction. Choose a unit vector x in that intersection. Then B x is zero, while A x has length at least sigma j. So A minus B has operator norm at least sigma j. Every approximation that uses fewer than j independent output directions must make an error of at least sigma j on some unit input. This is already half of the Eckart–Young theorem.

slides.title: What to reconstruct
slides.lead: Try proving the two singular-value games without naming any spectral theorem.
body: Use only the orthonormal singular bases, the formula for the squared output length, and the dimension-intersection inequality. Then take a three-dimensional diagonal map with singular values six, three, and one. Explain why discarding two input directions can reduce the largest surviving output length to one, but cannot reduce it below one. Finally, prove the kernel argument for a rank-one approximation. Ask yourself precisely where the dimension of the source appears, and why the dimension of the target does not enter the conclusion.
